kurals.tamil:
அரங்கின்றி வட்டாடி யற்றே நிரம்பிய
நூலின்றிக் கோட்டி கொளல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Arangindri vattaadi yatre nirampiya
Noolindrik kotti kolal.
kurals.meaning: To address an assembly of the learned without having fully mastered the texts of learning is like playing at dice without a board marked out.
kurals.elementary: Imagine trying to play a board game when nobody has drawn the board. You can roll the dice, but none of your moves mean anything. This kural says that speaking in front of wise people when you haven’t really studied is exactly like that: lots of movement, no real game.
kurals.university: The image is precise: vattu (dice or game pieces) moved without an arangu (the ruled board or square) produce motion without rules, and therefore without meaning or result. Kotti (an assembly, a learned gathering) is the arena of debate, and nirampiya nool (complete, fully mastered texts) is the board that gives structure to every move. Parimelazhagar reads the verse as a warning to one who enters discussion with no framework of learning: his words, however energetic, have nothing to be scored against. The chapter thus opens by defining ignorance not as silence but as ungrounded speech. Across traditions, the parallel concern is the would-be teacher or debater who speaks confidently while ‘understanding neither what they say’ (1 Timothy), the Qur’anic ban on pursuing what one has no knowledge of, and Plato’s critique of the rhetorician who persuades without knowing.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Bhagavad Gita 4.40 teaches that the ignorant person who lacks faith in the revealed scriptures and is full of doubt falls away, finding happiness neither in this world nor the next.
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes a person who has neither learned the scriptures nor trusts them; such a person has no stable ground to stand on and so cannot progress.
hinduism.tie_back: Both describe the person without a foundation of learning as having no framework — the Kural’s ‘board’ — so that nothing he does adds up.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Shares the idea that lack of scriptural grounding leaves one without footing, but the Gita’s focus is spiritual doubt, not public speaking in an assembly.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Desiring to be teachers of the law; understanding neither what they say, nor whereof they affirm.”
christianity.explanation: Paul warns Timothy about people who want the status of teachers even though they don’t understand the very things they speak about so confidently.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural’s figure exactly: someone who takes the floor in a learned setting without the learning that would give his words meaning.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close thematic match (unlearned would-be teachers speaking with confidence); lacks the Kural’s dice-board image.

islam.quote_or_event: “And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge. Indeed, the hearing, the sight and the heart - about all those [one] will be questioned.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an forbids following or asserting things one has no knowledge of, because every faculty used will be held to account.
islam.tie_back: Both condemn acting and speaking as if one knew, when there is no knowledge underneath.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong on the principle (do not act/speak without knowledge); broader than the Kural’s specific setting of a learned assembly.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs warns that jumping in to answer before one has properly heard and understood the matter is both foolish and shameful.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it describes speaking without the necessary grounding — and the public embarrassment that follows.
judaism._accuracy_note: Partial match: Proverbs targets hasty speech before hearing, the Kural targets speech without study. Both locate folly in ungrounded speaking.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Simile of the Snake, the Buddha describes people who learn the teaching poorly and use it only to criticize others and win debates, comparing them to someone who grabs a water snake by the tail and is bitten.
buddhism.explanation: Learning grasped badly and used for argument doesn’t help the arguer — it harms him, like picking up a snake the wrong way.
buddhism.tie_back: Both picture debate conducted without real mastery of the texts as a game that cannot be won.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. MN 22 concerns wrongly grasped learning used for debate; the Kural concerns lack of learning altogether. Related but not identical.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Phaethon insists on driving his father Helios’s sun-chariot without the skill for it; he loses control of the horses and scorches the earth before Zeus strikes him down.
greek_mythology.explanation: Phaethon takes on a role that needs mastery he doesn’t have, and his confident attempt turns into chaos.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like dice moved without a board, action without mastery produces motion with no order or good result.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Weak, analogical match: about presuming skill in general, not about speaking in a learned assembly. Best available myth.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s Gorgias, Socrates gets Gorgias to admit that the orator, who has no knowledge of medicine, can seem more convincing than the doctor to an ignorant audience — one who does not know persuading those who do not know.
philosophy.explanation: Socrates shows that rhetoric without knowledge only works in front of people who also don’t know; before experts it collapses.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural makes the same point about the unlearned speaker in an assembly of the learned: his performance has nothing to rest on.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Strong conceptual parallel (speaking without knowledge); Plato’s setting is persuasion of crowds rather than a learned assembly.

kurals.tamil:
கல்லாதான் சொற்கா முறுதல் முலையிரண்டும்
இல்லாதாள் பெண்காமுற் றற்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Kallaadhaan sorkaa murudhal mulaiyirandum
Illaadhaal penkaamut rattru.
kurals.meaning: For an unlearned man to long to be heard as a speaker is like a woman without breasts longing to be desired as a woman.
kurals.elementary: Some people want everyone to listen to them, but they haven’t learned anything worth saying. Valluvar uses a blunt comparison from his own time: it’s like wanting to be admired for something you simply don’t have. The wish is there, but the thing that would make it come true is missing.
kurals.university: Sorkaamurudhal is a craving for speech — specifically the desire to be admired for eloquence in an assembly. Valluvar’s simile, jarring to modern ears, is built on the conventions of classical Tamil poetics, where breasts are a standard marker of feminine attractiveness; the point is structural rather than a comment on women: a desire whose necessary basis is absent is futile and invites ridicule. Learning is to speech what that physical attribute is to erotic appeal in the poetic code. Parallel traditions frame the same pathology as the fool who ‘hath no delight in understanding, but that his heart may discover itself’ (Proverbs 18:2), the Gita’s ‘men of small knowledge’ attached to flowery words, and the Dhammapada’s reminder that one is not wise because one speaks much. Modern readers may note the simile’s gendered framing as a product of its poetic era.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Bhagavad Gita 2.42–43 describes people of little understanding who delight in the flowery words of the Vedas and declare that there is nothing beyond them.
hinduism.explanation: Krishna criticizes those who love impressive-sounding language but lack the understanding behind it.
hinduism.tie_back: Both portray a hunger for fine speech in someone who has not acquired the knowledge that would give it substance.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Shared theme of attachment to eloquent words without depth; the Gita addresses ritualists, not public speakers.

christianity.quote_or_event: “A fool hath no delight in understanding, but that his heart may discover itself.”
christianity.explanation: The fool isn’t interested in learning anything; he only wants a chance to show off what he thinks.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural’s unlearned man: all desire to be heard, no desire to learn.
christianity._accuracy_note: Very close: craving self-expression without understanding. The Kural adds the simile of futile desire.

islam.quote_or_event: “And of the people is he who disputes about Allah without knowledge or guidance or an enlightening book [from Him].”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an criticizes those who eagerly argue about the most serious matters even though they have no knowledge, no guidance, and no scripture behind them.
islam.tie_back: Both describe the urge to hold forth that is not matched by any learning.
islam._accuracy_note: Good match on speaking/arguing without knowledge; the Qur’an’s subject is theological dispute specifically.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A fool also is full of words.”
judaism.explanation: Ecclesiastes observes that the fool multiplies words, talking at length about things he cannot know.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s unlearned man likewise wants to fill the room with speech that has nothing behind it.
judaism._accuracy_note: Captures the fool’s excess of words; does not carry the Kural’s idea of a desire doomed by a missing prerequisite.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One is not wise because one speaks much. He who is peaceable, friendly and fearless is called wise.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada separates wisdom from talkativeness: speaking a lot is not what makes a person wise.
buddhism.tie_back: Both deny that eagerness to speak is any sign of learning.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong on speech ≠ wisdom; the Kural focuses on the futility of the desire itself.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The satyr Marsyas picks up the flute Athena had thrown away, becomes proud of his playing, and challenges Apollo to a musical contest; he loses and is flayed.
greek_mythology.explanation: Marsyas wanted to be admired as a master musician on the strength of a borrowed instrument and a little practice.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s unlearned speaker, he craves the standing of the accomplished without the full accomplishment, and is publicly humiliated.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Parallel of craving recognition without mastery; context is music and divine rivalry, not speech.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Apology, Socrates says he examined the poets and found that they could not explain their own poems, yet because of their poetry they believed themselves wise in other matters as well.
philosophy.explanation: The poets had fine words and wanted the reputation of wisdom, but their knowledge did not match their speech.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s speaker likewise wants to be admired for words that are not backed by learning.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a different Apology passage (the poets). Shared theme of eloquence without knowledge.

kurals.tamil:
கல்லா தவரும் நனிநல்லர் கற்றார்முன்
சொல்லா திருக்கப் பெறின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kallaa thavarum naninallar katraarmun
Sollaa thirukkap perin.
kurals.meaning: Even the unlearned are counted very good, if only they can keep from speaking in the presence of the learned.
kurals.elementary: If you don’t know much about a subject and you’re with experts, the smartest thing you can do is stay quiet and listen. People will actually think well of you for it. Talking would show what you don’t know; silence protects you and lets you learn.
kurals.university: The irony of nani nallar (‘exceedingly good’) is gentle but pointed: the unlearned person’s one available virtue is restraint. Parimelazhagar notes that silence both conceals the defect and avoids the harm of error. The verse inverts the previous kural — where the unlearned craved speech, here he is redeemed by abstaining from it. This is one of the most widely shared moral intuitions across cultures: Proverbs 17:28 (‘Even a fool, when he holdeth his peace, is counted wise’), Rabbi Akiva’s ‘a fence for wisdom is silence’, and the famous Sanskrit maxim of Bhartrhari that silence is the ornament of the unlearned in an assembly of scholars, which is an almost exact parallel. The Buddhist corpus adds the self-knowledge dimension: the fool who knows he is a fool is to that extent wise.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Bhartrhari’s Nitishataka says the Creator gave ignorance a covering that is entirely in one’s own control — silence — and that, especially in an assembly of the learned, silence is the ornament of the unlearned (vibhūṣaṇaṃ maunam apaṇḍitānām).
hinduism.explanation: The unlearned always have a way to hide their ignorance: simply to stay quiet, above all among scholars.
hinduism.tie_back: This is nearly the Kural word for word: among the learned, the unlearned are best off silent.
hinduism.source: Bhartrhari, Nitishataka, verse 7 (numbering varies by edition)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the Sanskrit; the final phrase is transliterated directly. Near one-to-one match in content and setting.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Even a fool, when he holdeth his peace, is counted wise: and he that shutteth his lips is esteemed a man of understanding.”
christianity.explanation: A foolish person who keeps quiet will be taken for wise, because no one hears anything foolish from him.
christianity.tie_back: Exactly the Kural’s claim: the unlearned become ‘very good’ by staying silent.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match; the Kural adds the specific setting of being ‘before the learned’.

islam.quote_or_event: “Anybody who believes in Allah and the Last Day should talk what is good or keep quiet.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet taught that a believer should either say something good or stay silent.
islam.tie_back: Both treat silence as the right course when one has nothing sound to contribute.
islam._accuracy_note: Quote is an excerpt of the final clause of a longer hadith. General ethic of speech; not specific to the unlearned before scholars.

judaism.quote_or_event: Rabbi Akiva teaches that silence is a protective fence around wisdom.
judaism.explanation: Just as a fence protects a field, keeping quiet protects and preserves wisdom.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural likewise makes silence the safeguard of the person who lacks learning.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase (translations vary: ‘a fence for wisdom is silence’). Akiva’s maxim is general; the Kural applies it to the unlearned.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “A fool who knows his foolishness is wise at least to that extent, but a fool who thinks himself wise is a fool indeed.”
buddhism.explanation: Recognizing one’s own ignorance is already a kind of wisdom; the real fool is the one who thinks he knows.
buddhism.tie_back: The unlearned person who stays quiet before the learned shows exactly this self-awareness, and so earns the Kural’s praise.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong on acknowledging ignorance; silence is implied rather than stated.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Diogenes Laertius reports that Pythagoras’s new pupils had to keep silence for five years, only listening to his discourses, before they were admitted to see him.
greek_mythology.explanation: In the Pythagorean school, beginners earned the right to speak by first listening in silence for a long time.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The same principle as the Kural: those who have not yet learned should be silent in the presence of those who have.
greek_mythology.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 8.10
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Greek legendary tradition (Pythagorean lore) rather than myth proper; strong on silence of the unlearned before the learned.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent.”
philosophy.explanation: Wittgenstein ends his Tractatus by saying that where language cannot meaningfully reach, one should not try to speak.
philosophy.tie_back: Both counsel silence at the boundary of what one can responsibly say, though Wittgenstein’s boundary is logical, not personal learning.
philosophy.source: Ludwig Wittgenstein, Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus, proposition 7 (tr. C. K. Ogden)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Weak match: Wittgenstein’s limit is what language can express, not what an individual has learned. Included as the best-known philosophical maxim on principled silence.

kurals.tamil:
கல்லாதான் ஒட்பம் கழியநன் றாயினும்
கொள்ளார் அறிவுடை யார்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kallaadhaan otpam kazhiyanan raayinum
Kollaar arivudai yaar.
kurals.meaning: Even if an unlearned man’s cleverness happens to be exceedingly good, the wise will not accept it as sound.
kurals.elementary: Sometimes a person who never studied says something that sounds really smart. Wise people still don’t rely on it, because it’s a lucky hit, not something the person truly understands. Next time the same person may be completely wrong, and they won’t know the difference.
kurals.university: Otpam denotes native sharpness or cleverness; kazhiya nandru (‘exceedingly good’) concedes that it may even be impressive. Yet the wise (arivudaiyaar) do not ‘take’ (kollaar) it. Parimelazhagar’s explanation is epistemic: insight not grounded in learning is accidental and unreliable, so it cannot be built upon. This anticipates Plato’s distinction in the Meno between true opinion and knowledge — right opinions are valuable but ‘run away’ unless tied down by reasoning, like the statues of Daedalus. The kural is harder-edged than some traditions would allow: Pirkei Avot’s ‘look not at the vessel but at what is in it’ pushes the other way, and Cassandra’s myth dramatizes the tragedy of truth rejected because of its source. The accuracy notes below mark these as contrasts.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Bhagavad Gita 4.34 instructs the seeker to learn the truth by approaching a spiritual master with humility, inquiry and service, because those who have seen the truth can impart knowledge.
hinduism.explanation: Real knowledge is to be received from those who have studied and realized it, not picked up from anyone who sounds clever.
hinduism.tie_back: Both locate reliable insight in those grounded in learning, which is why the wise do not rely on the unlearned.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Indirect: the Gita affirms learning from the realized rather than explicitly rejecting the insights of the unlearned.

christianity.quote_or_event: “The legs of the lame are not equal: so is a parable in the mouth of fools.”
christianity.explanation: A wise saying in the mouth of a fool is as unsteady as a lame person’s walk; it doesn’t carry him anywhere.
christianity.tie_back: Even a good saying from one without understanding is not something to lean on — the Kural’s very point.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good match on wisdom being unreliable in a fool’s mouth; Proverbs stresses the fool’s misuse, the Kural the listener’s refusal.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, if there comes to you a disobedient one with information, investigate, lest you harm a people out of ignorance and become, over what you have done, regretful.”
islam.explanation: Information from an unreliable source is not to be accepted at face value; it must be checked first.
islam.tie_back: Both teach that the reliability of the source matters, and the wise do not simply accept what comes from an unqualified one.
islam._accuracy_note: Partial: the Qur’an’s unreliable source is morally untrustworthy (fasiq), not unlearned, and it counsels verification rather than rejection.

judaism.quote_or_event: Rabbi Meir says: look not at the vessel but at what is in it — a new jug may be full of old wine, and an old jug may not even contain new wine.
judaism.explanation: Judge a teaching by its content rather than by the status of the one who delivers it.
judaism.tie_back: This is a contrast: the Mishnah urges weighing content on its merits, while the Kural says the wise will not trust even good-seeming insight from the unlearned.
judaism._accuracy_note: Contrast rather than parallel. Included honestly because no close Jewish parallel was found; it frames the tension the Kural resolves the other way.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Though all his life a fool associates with a wise man, he no more comprehends the Truth than a spoon tastes the flavour of the soup.”
buddhism.explanation: A fool may be surrounded by wisdom and even handle it, as a spoon handles soup, without ever tasting its meaning.
buddhism.tie_back: The unlearned person’s clever-sounding insight is like soup on a spoon: present, but not understood — so the wise do not rely on it.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Indirect: the verse is about the fool’s failure to understand, which grounds (but does not state) the Kural’s point about the wise not accepting his insight.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Cassandra is given the gift of prophecy by Apollo but cursed so that no one believes her; her true warnings about Troy and Agamemnon’s murder are ignored.
greek_mythology.explanation: Cassandra speaks the truth, but her hearers dismiss it because of who she is and how she speaks.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A cautionary counterpoint: the Kural says the wise will not trust the unlearned even when they are right; Cassandra shows the cost when a true word is rejected for its source.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Contrast/complication rather than parallel; Cassandra is inspired, not unlearned. Best available myth on truth disregarded because of its source.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Meno, Socrates says true opinions are like the statues of Daedalus: valuable while they stay, but they run away unless tied down by reasoning, and once tied they become knowledge.
philosophy.explanation: Someone can be right by luck, but without the understanding that fixes it in place, their correct opinion cannot be relied upon.
philosophy.tie_back: This is precisely why the wise do not ‘take’ the unlearned man’s cleverness: it is right opinion without the tether of learning.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Very strong conceptual parallel (unreliability of untethered correct opinion).

kurals.tamil:
கல்லா ஒருவன் தகைமை தலைப்பெய்து
சொல்லாடச் சோர்வு படும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kallaa oruvan thagaimai thalaippeydhu
Sollaadach chorvu padum.
kurals.meaning: The self-esteem of an unlearned man will wither away as soon as he meets and converses with the learned.
kurals.elementary: Someone might think they’re very smart — until they start talking with people who have actually studied. Then, very quickly, it becomes clear how little they know, and their proud image falls apart.
kurals.university: Thagaimai is estimation or worth — here the self-estimation (or reputation) that the unlearned man carries; thalaippeydhu means ‘meeting, coming face to face’ (with the learned), and chorvu padum ‘will droop, fail’. The kural completes the logic of 402–403: the man who does not keep silent will be exposed in conversation. This is the drama of the Socratic elenchus, where confident interlocutors are shown in dialogue to lack what they claimed; Plato’s Phaedrus names the result ‘the show of wisdom without the reality’. The Mundaka and Katha Upanishads describe fools ‘wise in their own conceit’, and 1 Corinthians 8:2 compresses the diagnosis into a sentence. Dhammapada 63’s ‘fool who thinks himself wise’ is exactly the figure whose pride collapses here.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Mundaka Upanishad describes fools who live in ignorance yet consider themselves wise and learned; they wander about, afflicted, like the blind led by the blind.
hinduism.explanation: People who believe themselves learned while remaining ignorant stumble from one error to another.
hinduism.tie_back: Both portray the false self-estimation of the unlearned, which cannot survive contact with reality.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Strong on self-deceived pseudo-learning; the Upanishad does not specify exposure through conversation.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And if any man think that he knoweth any thing, he knoweth nothing yet as he ought to know.”
christianity.explanation: Paul warns that the person who is sure of his own knowledge has not yet begun to know as he should.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s unlearned man thinks highly of himself; Paul explains why that confidence is empty.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong on false self-estimation; lacks the Kural’s scene of exposure before the learned.

islam.quote_or_event: “Here you are - those who have argued about that of which you have [some] knowledge, but why do you argue about that of which you have no knowledge? And Allah knows, while you know not.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an rebukes people who push their arguments into areas where they have no knowledge at all.
islam.tie_back: Both picture the unlearned entering debate and being shown up for lacking the knowledge they pretend to.
islam._accuracy_note: Close on arguing without knowledge being exposed; the Qur’anic context is a specific dispute about Abraham.

judaism.quote_or_event: Pirkei Avot lists seven marks of the wise person — among them, he does not speak before one greater in wisdom, does not interrupt, is not hasty to answer, and admits when he has not heard something — while the unformed person (golem) does the opposite.
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah contrasts how the wise and the unformed behave in conversation with the learned.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s unlearned man behaves like the golem and is exposed in the very kind of conversation the Mishnah describes.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Close setting (conduct in learned conversation); framed as a behavioral contrast rather than a prediction of collapse.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “A fool who knows his foolishness is wise at least to that extent, but a fool who thinks himself wise is a fool indeed.”
buddhism.explanation: The worst kind of fool is the one who believes he is wise.
buddhism.tie_back: That self-believing fool is exactly the man whose esteem collapses when he talks with the learned.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong on false self-estimation; the Kural adds the moment of public exposure.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When King Midas, judging a music contest, loudly declared Pan’s rustic piping superior to Apollo’s lyre, Apollo gave him the ears of an ass to show the quality of his judgment.
greek_mythology.explanation: Midas spoke up confidently among those who truly knew music, and his lack of understanding was made visible to all.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s unlearned man, Midas’s standing collapses the moment he offers his opinion in a company of experts.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Good narrative parallel of ignorance exposed by speaking out among the skilled.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “They will appear to be omniscient and will generally know nothing; they will be tiresome company, having the show of wisdom without the reality.”
philosophy.explanation: King Thamus warns that writing will let people seem knowledgeable without real understanding.
philosophy.tie_back: ‘The show of wisdom without the reality’ is exactly the unlearned man’s self-image that wilts in real conversation — which, for Plato, is where real knowledge is tested.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong on seeming-versus-real wisdom; Plato’s immediate target is reliance on writing.

kurals.tamil:
உளரென்னும் மாத்திரையர் அல்லால் பயவாக்
களரனையர் கல்லா தவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Ularennum maaththiraiyar allaal payavaak
Kalaranaiyar kallaa thavar.
kurals.meaning: The unlearned can only be said to exist; beyond that, they are like barren saline land that yields nothing.
kurals.elementary: Some land is so salty that nothing grows on it, no matter how much rain falls. Valluvar says a person who never learns is like that land: they are there, alive, but nothing useful grows from them for themselves or anyone else.
kurals.university: Ularennum maaththiraiyar — ‘mere measure of existing’ — reduces the unlearned to bare presence. Kalar is saline or alkaline soil, proverbial in Tamil for barrenness; payavaa (‘unyielding’) insists on the absence of any fruit. The agricultural image makes learning the cultivation that turns land into field. Striking parallels exist: the Buddha’s Desana Sutta (SN 42.7) speaks of a field that is ‘salty’ and poor as the worst kind of soil; the hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari 79 compares recipients of knowledge to types of land, including barren land that neither holds water nor grows anything; Jeremiah 17:6 speaks of ‘a salt land and not inhabited’; Hesiod calls the man who neither thinks nor learns ‘unprofitable’; and Seneca’s ‘leisure without study is death… a tomb for the living man’ matches the Kural’s reduction of such a life to mere existence.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Hitopadesha asks what use is a son who is born but is neither learned nor virtuous — like a blind eye, which brings only pain.
hinduism.explanation: A life without learning, even in a family, is compared to an organ that is present but useless.
hinduism.tie_back: Both reduce the unlearned person to mere presence without benefit — existing, but yielding nothing.
hinduism.source: Hitopadesha, Prastavika (Introduction), verse on the unlearned son
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; verse numbering varies by edition. Strong on ‘present but useless’; the image is a blind eye, not barren land.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Behold, these three years I come seeking fruit on this fig tree, and find none: cut it down; why cumbereth it the ground?”
christianity.explanation: In Jesus’s parable, a fig tree that bears no fruit year after year is judged to be merely taking up space.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s unlearned person likewise merely occupies the ground, yielding nothing.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good image of fruitless existence; the parable is about repentance rather than learning.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet compared the guidance and knowledge sent through him to abundant rain falling on land: some fertile soil absorbs it and grows vegetation, some holds water for others, and “a portion of it was barren which could neither hold the water nor bring forth vegetation.”
islam.explanation: People respond to knowledge like different kinds of land; some benefit themselves and others, while some remain barren.
islam.tie_back: An almost identical image: the one who takes in no knowledge is barren land that yields nothing.
islam._accuracy_note: Mostly paraphrase with one verbatim phrase in quotation marks. Very close image (barren land ↔ one who does not take in knowledge).

judaism.quote_or_event: “For he shall be like the heath in the desert, and shall not see when good cometh; but shall inhabit the parched places in the wilderness, in a salt land and not inhabited.”
judaism.explanation: Jeremiah compares a spiritually cut-off person to a shrub in salty, barren ground where nothing good comes.
judaism.tie_back: The same ‘salt land’ image the Kural uses for the unlearned.
judaism._accuracy_note: Striking verbal parallel (salt land), but Jeremiah’s subject is the one who trusts in man rather than God, not the unlearned.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Desana Sutta the Buddha compares three fields — excellent, middling, and one that is poor, hard, salty, with bad soil — to three kinds of listeners to his teaching.
buddhism.explanation: The same seed does very differently depending on the ground; the salty, poor field yields least.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural uses the same image of saline, unproductive soil for the person who has not taken in learning.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Very close image; but the Buddha still teaches the ‘salty field’ out of compassion, so the moral emphasis differs.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod says the best man thinks things through for himself, the next best listens to good advice, but the man who neither thinks for himself nor takes to heart what another tells him is an unprofitable man.
greek_mythology.explanation: The person who neither reasons nor learns from others is of no use.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Both call the unlearned person ‘unyielding’ or ‘unprofitable’ — present but without fruit.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Archaic Greek wisdom poetry rather than myth; close in judgment (‘unprofitable’).

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Leisure without study is death; it is a tomb for the living man.”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca says a life with free time but no study is not truly living — it is a kind of burial while still alive.
philosophy.tie_back: Just as the Kural says the unlearned merely ‘exist’, Seneca says a life without learning is death in life.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 82.3 (tr. R. M. Gummere)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong match on life without learning as mere existence; Seneca speaks of leisure specifically.

kurals.tamil:
நுண்மாண் நுழைபுலம் இல்லான் எழில்நலம்
மண்மாண் புனைபாவை யற்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Nunmaan nuzhaipulam illaan ezhilnalam
Manmaan punaipaavai yattru.
kurals.meaning: The fine looks of one who lacks subtle, penetrating understanding are like those of a beautifully painted doll made of clay.
kurals.elementary: A clay doll can be painted to look wonderful, but there is nothing inside it — it can’t think. Valluvar says a good-looking person who hasn’t developed a sharp, curious mind is like that doll: nice to look at, but empty.
kurals.university: Nunmaan nuzhaipulam — ‘subtle, excellent, penetrating intellect’ — names the kind of understanding that learning produces, able to enter into (nuzhai) fine distinctions. Its absence makes ezhil nalam (beauty, handsomeness) into manmaan punai paavai: a clay figure elaborately decorated. The contrast is surface versus interior. Aesop’s fox, finding an actor’s mask, puts it memorably: a beautiful head, but no brains. Chanakya Niti 3.8 is an almost perfect Sanskrit parallel — beauty, youth and noble birth without learning are like scentless kimshuka flowers. The Qur’an describes those whose ‘forms please you’ as ‘pieces of wood propped up’, and Proverbs likens beauty without discretion to a gold ring in a swine’s snout.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Chanakya Niti says that those endowed with beauty and youth and born in great families, if devoid of learning, do not shine — like kimshuka flowers that have no fragrance.
hinduism.explanation: Looks, youth and noble birth are not enough; without learning, a person is like a bright flower with no scent.
hinduism.tie_back: An almost exact parallel: outward beauty without learning is hollow.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the Sanskrit. Near one-to-one match; the image is a scentless flower rather than a clay doll.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye are like unto whited sepulchres, which indeed appear beautiful outward, but are within full of dead men’s bones, and of all uncleanness.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus condemns those who look impressive outside while being empty or corrupt inside.
christianity.tie_back: Both contrast a beautiful exterior with a lifeless interior.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shares the outer-beauty/inner-emptiness structure; Jesus’s target is moral hypocrisy, not lack of intellect.

islam.quote_or_event: “And when you see them, their forms please you, and if they speak, you listen to their speech. [They are] as if they were pieces of wood propped up.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes people whose appearance impresses, but who are inwardly like lifeless timber leaning against a wall.
islam.tie_back: Very close to the Kural’s decorated clay doll: an attractive form with nothing living inside.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong image match; the Qur’anic subject is the hypocrites’ lack of faith and understanding, not learning as such.

judaism.quote_or_event: “As a jewel of gold in a swine’s snout, so is a fair woman which is without discretion.”
judaism.explanation: Beauty without good sense is as incongruous and wasted as a gold ring in a pig’s nose.
judaism.tie_back: Both say that outward beauty is worthless without inner understanding.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close structural match (beauty minus discernment); Proverbs speaks of a woman, the Kural of anyone.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada asks us to look at the body as a painted image, a mass of sores held together, sickly and full of plans that do not last.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha urges looking past the attractive, decorated surface of the body to see how fragile it really is.
buddhism.tie_back: The same ‘painted image’ idea as the Kural’s decorated clay doll: outward beauty that hides emptiness.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Shared image of a painted figure; the Buddhist point is impermanence of the body, not lack of learning.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aesop’s fable, a fox rummaging in an actor’s house finds a beautifully made mask and remarks that it is a fine head, but it has no brains.
greek_mythology.explanation: The mask looks perfect, but there’s nothing inside it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Almost the Kural’s exact image: a beautiful crafted head, empty of mind.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop’s Fables, ‘The Fox and the Mask’ (Perry 27)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; wording varies across translations. Greek fable tradition rather than myth proper. Near-exact image match.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Charmides, when everyone admires the young Charmides’ beauty, Socrates asks whether he also has a noble soul, proposing to ‘strip’ and examine that before his body.
philosophy.explanation: Socrates redirects attention from a handsome appearance to the quality of the mind within.
philosophy.tie_back: Both hold that physical beauty is of little worth unless the mind within is refined.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Good match on priority of mind over looks; Charmides turns out to be promising, unlike the Kural’s subject.

kurals.tamil:
நல்லார்கண் பட்ட வறுமையின் இன்னாதே
கல்லார்கண் பட்ட திரு.
kurals.transliteration:
Nallaarkan patta varumaiyin innaadhe
Kallaarkan patta thiru.
kurals.meaning: Wealth that falls into the hands of the unlearned brings more misery than poverty that falls upon the good.
kurals.elementary: It’s sad when good, wise people are poor. But Valluvar says it’s even worse when foolish, unlearned people get lots of money — because they don’t know how to use it well, and they can cause harm to themselves and everyone around them.
kurals.university: Innaadhu (painful, harmful) is the operative comparative: both situations are bad, but thiru (wealth, fortune) in the hands of the unlearned (kallaar) is worse than poverty befalling the good (nallaar). Parimelazhagar explains that the learned poor still do good and are not diminished, whereas the unlearned rich use wealth for harm. The verse belongs to Porul’s concern with statecraft: resources without wisdom are a public danger. Plato’s Euthydemus argues that wealth and other ‘goods’ are good only under the guidance of wisdom and become greater evils under ignorance; the Dhammapada says riches ruin the foolish; the Qur’an forbids handing property to the weak-minded; and Ecclesiastes laments folly set in great dignity.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Hitopadesha teaches that learning gives humility; from humility comes worthiness; from worthiness, wealth; from wealth, righteous action; and from that, happiness.
hinduism.explanation: In the right order, wealth should come after and through learning, so that it leads to good use and true happiness.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural shows what goes wrong when that order is broken and wealth reaches someone without learning.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; verse numbering varies. Indirect: states the ideal sequence rather than the harm of wealth without learning.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But God said unto him, Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided?”
christianity.explanation: In the parable of the rich fool, a man piles up wealth without wisdom about what truly matters, and it does him no good.
christianity.tie_back: Both show wealth in the hands of a fool as something that ends in loss rather than blessing.
christianity._accuracy_note: The ‘fool’ here lacks spiritual wisdom rather than learning; no comparison with the poverty of the good.

islam.quote_or_event: “And do not give the weak-minded your property, which Allah has made a means of sustenance for you, but provide for them with it and clothe them and speak to them words of appropriate kindness.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an instructs that wealth should not be handed over to those who lack the judgment to manage it.
islam.tie_back: Both recognize that wealth in the control of the unwise is harmful.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong on wealth being unsafe with the ‘weak-minded’ (sufaha); lacks the comparison with virtuous poverty.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Better is the poor that walketh in his integrity, than he that is perverse in his lips, and is a fool.”
judaism.explanation: A poor person of integrity is better off than a foolish one who speaks crookedly.
judaism.tie_back: Both set the poverty of the good above the condition of the fool.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close structure (good poor vs. fool); the fool’s wealth is implied (cf. Prov 28:6), not stated.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Riches ruin only the foolish, not those in quest of the Beyond. By craving for riches the witless man ruins himself as well as others.”
buddhism.explanation: Wealth itself is not the problem; it destroys those who lack wisdom, and they drag others down too.
buddhism.tie_back: Exactly the Kural’s concern: wealth in the hands of the unwise causes harm.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close; lacks only the explicit comparison with the poverty of the good.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: King Midas foolishly asks Dionysus that everything he touches turn to gold; soon his food and drink become gold and he begs to be freed of the gift.
greek_mythology.explanation: Midas gets unlimited wealth but lacks the wisdom to want it rightly, and it becomes a curse.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The classic picture of wealth becoming misery in the hands of a fool.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Strong image of wealth harming the unwise; no contrast with the virtuous poor.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Euthydemus, Socrates argues that wealth, health and other so-called goods are not good in themselves: guided by wisdom they are greater goods, but under ignorance they are greater evils.
philosophy.explanation: What makes wealth good or bad is whether it is used with wisdom or without it.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the philosophical ground of the Kural: wealth in the hands of the unlearned becomes a greater evil than poverty.

kurals.tamil:
மேற்பிறந்தா ராயினும் கல்லாதார் கீழ்ப்பிறந்தும்
கற்றார் அனைத்திலர் பாடு.
kurals.transliteration:
Merpirandhaa raayinum kallaadhaar keezhppirandhum
Katraar anaiththilar paadu.
kurals.meaning: Though born in a high station, the unlearned do not have the worth of the learned who are born in a low one.
kurals.elementary: Some people think being born into an important family makes them better than others. Valluvar disagrees: a person from a humble family who has learned a lot is worth more than a high-born person who hasn’t learned anything. What you learn matters more than where you were born.
kurals.university: Merpirandhaar/keezhppirandhu (born high/born low) refers to the social hierarchy of birth in Valluvar’s world; paadu is dignity, worth or standing. The kural does not abolish hierarchy in theory but subordinates it to learning in practice, a notable move in a society structured by birth. The closest parallel is Mishnah Horayot 3:8: a mamzer who is a Torah scholar takes precedence over a High Priest who is ignorant. Buddhism’s Dhammapada 393 and the Vasala Sutta reject birth as the measure of a brahmin; the Upanishadic story of Satyakama Jabala shows a boy of unknown lineage accepted for his truthfulness; Plato’s myth of the metals places each child by the quality of soul, not parentage; and Ecclesiastes prefers a poor, wise youth to a foolish king.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Satyakama Jabala, who does not know his father’s lineage, honestly tells the sage Gautama so; Gautama accepts him as a student, saying only a true brahmin would speak such truth, and Satyakama becomes a great teacher.
hinduism.explanation: A boy of unknown and humble birth is admitted to learning because of his character, and rises to eminence through it.
hinduism.tie_back: Both place the worth gained through truth and learning above the accident of birth.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Strong on birth yielding to merit; the Upanishad’s criterion is truthfulness, leading to learning.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Better is a poor and a wise child than an old and foolish king, who will no more be admonished.”
christianity.explanation: A poor but wise young person is worth more than a king who has grown foolish and will not learn.
christianity.tie_back: Both rank wisdom from a low station above folly in a high one.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close match; Ecclesiastes contrasts wealth/office rather than birth, and is shared Hebrew Bible text.

islam.quote_or_event: “Allah will raise those who have believed among you and those who were given knowledge, by degrees.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an says true rank before God comes through faith and knowledge.
islam.tie_back: Both locate a person’s real standing in knowledge rather than in lineage.
islam._accuracy_note: Excerpt of the verse. Affirms elevation by knowledge; does not explicitly compare it with birth (cf. 49:13).

judaism.quote_or_event: The Mishnah sets an order of precedence by lineage — priest, Levite, Israelite, and so on down to the mamzer — but adds that if the mamzer is a Torah scholar and the High Priest is ignorant, the scholar-mamzer takes precedence over the ignorant High Priest.
judaism.explanation: Learning in Torah overrides even the highest birth-based rank.
judaism.tie_back: An almost exact parallel: the learned of lowest birth outrank the unlearned of highest birth.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Near one-to-one match in structure and meaning.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Not by matted hair, nor by lineage, nor by birth does one become a brahmin. But he in whom truth and righteousness exist, he is pure, he is a brahmin.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha redefines the highest social title as something earned by inner qualities, not inherited.
buddhism.tie_back: Both deny that birth determines worth.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong on rejecting birth-based worth; the Buddha’s criterion is truth and righteousness rather than learning.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the ancient Life of Aesop, Aesop is a slave of lowly origin whose wit repeatedly outshines his master, the philosopher Xanthus, and who eventually wins his freedom and advises kings.
greek_mythology.explanation: A man of the lowest social position proves wiser than his socially superior, supposedly learned master.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s point dramatized: worth comes from understanding, not station of birth.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Greek popular legend rather than myth; Aesop’s wisdom is native wit rather than formal learning.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Republic’s ‘noble lie’ of the metals, Socrates says children may be born with a different metal from their parents — gold from bronze or bronze from gold — and each must be placed according to the quality of their soul, not their parentage.
philosophy.explanation: Plato’s ideal city ranks people by what they are capable of, not by the family they come from.
philosophy.tie_back: Both subordinate birth to cultivated capacity.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Plato’s criterion is natural capacity (then trained), close to but not identical with learning.

kurals.tamil:
விலங்கொடு மக்கள் அனையர் இலங்குநூல்
கற்றாரோடு ஏனை யவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Vilangodu makkal anaiyar ilangunool
Katraarodu enai yavar.
kurals.meaning: As beasts are compared with human beings, so are the unlearned compared with those who have studied illustrious works.
kurals.elementary: Think of how different a person is from an animal. Valluvar says the difference between someone who has studied great books and someone who hasn’t is just as big. Learning is what makes us fully human.
kurals.university: The closing kural states the chapter’s thesis as a proportion: learned : unlearned :: humans : animals. Ilangu nool (‘shining, illustrious texts’) specifies that it is serious learning, not mere literacy, that marks the difference. The analogy draws on a long tradition, shared across cultures, that locates the distinctively human in reason and cultivated understanding. Bhartrhari’s Nitishataka 12 says one devoid of literature, music and art is a beast without tail and horns; Aristotle, asked how the educated differ from the uneducated, replied ‘as much as the living from the dead’; Psalm 49:20 compares the man in honour without understanding to the beasts that perish; the Qur’an (7:179) likens those who do not use their hearts to understand to livestock; and the Dhammapada’s man of little learning grows old ‘like a bull’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Bhartrhari says a man devoid of literature, music and the arts is truly a beast, only without a tail and horns — and it is the animals’ great good fortune that he does not also eat grass.
hinduism.explanation: Without cultivated learning and art, a human being is really an animal in human shape.
hinduism.tie_back: Almost exactly the Kural’s proportion between the learned and the unlearned.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the Sanskrit. Near one-to-one match; Bhartrhari adds music and art to literature.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But these speak evil of those things which they know not: but what they know naturally, as brute beasts, in those things they corrupt themselves.”
christianity.explanation: Jude describes people who talk about what they don’t understand and know only what brute beasts know by instinct.
christianity.tie_back: Both compare those without understanding to animals.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shares the animal comparison for the ignorant; Jude’s subject is moral corruption of false teachers.

islam.quote_or_event: “They have hearts with which they do not understand, they have eyes with which they do not see, and they have ears with which they do not hear. Those are like livestock; rather, they are more astray.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an says people who do not use their faculties to understand are like cattle — or even worse off.
islam.tie_back: The same comparison: failing to cultivate understanding reduces a human to the level of animals.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong match on animal analogy for those without understanding; Qur’anic context is spiritual heedlessness.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Man that is in honour, and understandeth not, is like the beasts that perish.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist says that a person, even one of high standing, who lacks understanding is no better than an animal.
judaism.tie_back: Very close to the Kural: without understanding, humans are like beasts.
judaism.source: Psalm 49:20 (Hebrew Bible; KJV wording; Ps 49:21 in Hebrew numbering)
judaism._accuracy_note: Close; ‘understanding’ in the psalm is spiritual insight into mortality rather than book learning.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The man of little learning grows old like a bull. He grows only in bulk, but, his wisdom does not grow.”
buddhism.explanation: Someone who does not learn only gets older and bigger, like an ox — never wiser.
buddhism.tie_back: Both compare the unlearned to an animal.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close; the Dhammapada’s ‘little learning’ (appassuta) matches the Kural’s lack of study.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Circe turns Odysseus’s companions into swine, though their minds remain as before; Odysseus alone is protected by the herb moly, which Hermes gives him along with knowledge of how to resist her.
greek_mythology.explanation: Those without the protecting knowledge are reduced to animals; the one who has it remains fully human.
greek_mythology.tie_back: An allegorical parallel: lack of knowledge leaves a person reduced to the level of beasts.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Allegorical reading (moly as knowledge/reason is an ancient interpretation, not Homer’s explicit claim).

philosophy.quote_or_event: Asked how much the educated are superior to the uneducated, Aristotle replied: “As much as the living are to the dead.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says the gap between the educated and the uneducated is as great as the gap between life and death.
philosophy.tie_back: The same proportional form as the Kural, with living/dead in place of humans/animals.
philosophy.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 5.19 (tr. R. D. Hicks)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one structural match; wording of the reply varies slightly between translations (‘from the dead’ / ‘to the dead’).
